nameStory: Tatarian dogwood gets its name from Tataria, an old European term for the vast region of Siberia and Central Asia where this hardy shrub originates. Like other dogwoods, the 'dog' part likely comes from 'dag' or 'dagger,' referring to the hard wood that was once used to make sharp tools and skewers.
description: Tatarian dogwood is a tough, spreading shrub that can grow up to 10 feet tall, though it's often kept smaller in gardens. This cold-hardy plant is most famous for its brilliant red stems that practically glow against winter snow. Originally from Siberia and northern Asia, it's planted throughout New England as an ornamental shrub that thrives in our harsh winters. The plant produces clusters of small white flowers in spring and white berries in fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are bright coral-red to deep red, especially vivid in winter and early spring - they almost seem to glow against snow and look smooth to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are arranged in opposite pairs along the stems, with prominent curved veins that arc toward the leaf tip - feel smooth and slightly thick

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers appear in flat-topped clusters in late spring, each tiny flower having four petals

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: White berries ripen in late summer, sometimes with a slight blue tint - they feel firm and are about the size of small peas

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense thickets by sending up new shoots (suckers) from the base, creating colonies of red-stemmed shrubs

habitat: In New England, Tatarian dogwood is found almost exclusively in cultivated settings like parks, residential landscapes, and botanical gardens, as it's primarily grown as an ornamental plant. It thrives in moist, well-drained soils but is extremely adaptable to various conditions. With only one recorded observation in New England, it's quite rare in the wild here.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green, and clusters of small white flowers bloom in late spring. The red bark color begins to fade slightly as the plant puts energy into new growth.
seasonality.summer: Full green foliage masks the stems, and white berries begin forming after flowers fade. The plant looks like a typical green shrub during this season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, and white berries ripen fully. As temperatures drop, the stem color begins intensifying again.
seasonality.winter: This is showtime - with leaves gone, the brilliant red stems are fully exposed and most vibrant against snow. The bare red branches are the plant's signature feature.

funFact: Gardeners actually cut Tatarian dogwood stems down to the ground every few years on purpose - the youngest shoots produce the most brilliant red color, so this 'coppicing' keeps the winter display spectacular!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with red osier dogwood, which also has red stems. Remember that red osier is native and common near wetlands, while Tatarian dogwood is typically found only in landscaped areas and has slightly more orange-red stems.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - this isn't from Tatarstan specifically, but from the broader region once called Tataria. Many garden centers sell this under various names including 'Siberian dogwood' or simply 'red-twig dogwood,' which can cause confusion with our native red osier dogwood.
compareHints: Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands. Unlike flowering dogwood with its showy spring bracts, Tatarian has small, inconspicuous flower clusters. Its suckering habit also distinguishes it from tree-form dogwoods like flowering dogwood.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
